fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. Ezekiel looks up and sees the likeness of a throne, and then the LORD speaks to the man clothed in linen. The words are a command: "Go inside the wheelwork beneath the cherubim." (Ezekiel 10:2) The LORD is the one giving the orders.

I get why a priest came to mind, friend, since this is all happening around the temple. But the text has no priest speaking here. It says, "…the LORD said to the man clothed in linen…" (Ezekiel 10:2) The one giving the command is the LORD.

No watchman shows up in this scene, baker. Ezekiel sees the likeness of a throne above the cherubim. Then he reports, "…the LORD said to the man clothed in linen…" (Ezekiel 10:2) So the speaker is the LORD, not a watchman.
True, baker. The LORD says to fill his hands with burning coals and "…scatter them over the city." (Ezekiel 10:2) The coals have somewhere to go. They are meant for the city.

It's actually true, friend, so this one didn't hold. The LORD tells the man to fill his hands with burning coals and "…scatter them over the city." (Ezekiel 10:2) That's the command he's given. So the statement is true.

The city wall isn't mentioned in this passage, baker. The glory of the LORD rises from above the cherubim and stands "…over the threshold of the temple." (Ezekiel 10:4) The threshold is the spot the text names.

Close, baker, but this one points the opposite way. The text says "…the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the LORD." (Ezekiel 10:4) There's a cloud, yes, but the court is full of brightness. Darkness isn't what Ezekiel reports.
Yes, baker, voice. The sound of the wings is "…like the voice of God Almighty when He speaks." (Ezekiel 10:5) And that sound of the wings could be heard as far as the outer court.

Breath isn't the word Ezekiel uses, friend. He says the sound of the wings is "…like the voice of God Almighty when He speaks." (Ezekiel 10:5) That sound of the wings could be heard as far as the outer court.

Seraphim are a fair guess, baker, but this passage never mentions them. It says, "…one of the cherubim reached out his hand and took some of the fire that was among them." (Ezekiel 10:7) The one who hands over the fire is one of the cherubim.
False is right, friend. After the cherub puts the fire in his hands, the man clothed in linen "…received it and went out." (Ezekiel 10:7) He doesn't stay among the cherubim.

Yes, baker. Ezekiel says, "…they would go in any of the four directions, without turning as they moved." (Ezekiel 10:11) Four directions and no turning. Meanwhile I need three tries to get around my own counter.
Backing up isn't mentioned, baker. The text says they would go in any of the four directions "…without turning as they moved." (Ezekiel 10:11) So the answer is that they go without turning.

True, baker. The text says, "…wherever the head faced, the cherubim would go in that direction, without turning as they moved." (Ezekiel 10:11) Wherever the head faces, that's the direction they go. And they don't turn to do it.
It's actually true, friend. The text says, "…wherever the head faced, the cherubim would go in that direction…" (Ezekiel 10:11) They go in the direction the head faces.

Gates do come up in this passage, friend, but they're not covered in eyes. The text says the cherubim's bodies were full of eyes all around, "…as were their four wheels." (Ezekiel 10:12) The eyes are on the wheels.

That's the pair, baker. Ezekiel says each of the cherubim had four faces: "…the first face was that of a cherub, the second that of a man, the third that of a lion, and the fourth that of an eagle." (Ezekiel 10:14) That's four faces on every one of them.

A bear and a dove would make quite a pair, friend, but they're not in the text. The first two faces are a cherub and a man. Then the text says "…the third that of a lion, and the fourth that of an eagle." (Ezekiel 10:14) So the other two are a lion and an eagle.
True, baker. Ezekiel says, "These were the living creatures I had seen by the River Kebar." (Ezekiel 10:15) He had seen them before, at the River Kebar. This isn't his first time.

That's it, baker. "…the glory of the LORD moved away from the threshold of the temple and stood above the cherubim." (Ezekiel 10:18) It leaves the threshold and stands above them. Then the cherubim lift their wings and rise (Ezekiel 10:19).

The court was filled with the brightness of the glory earlier (Ezekiel 10:4), baker. But in this verse the glory moves away from the threshold and "…stood above the cherubim." (Ezekiel 10:18) The text says it stands above the cherubim, so that's the answer.

Yes, baker. The text says, "…they stopped at the entrance of the east gate of the house of the LORD, with the glory of the God of Israel above them." (Ezekiel 10:19) The glory of the God of Israel is above them as they stop. The wheels are beside them as they go.
Close, baker, but the count is off. The text says, "Each had four faces and four wings…" (Ezekiel 10:21) That's four wings, not six.
